parole.significato: Converts certain words to faux Italian or Spanish. Can be used with Spanish el for expressions such as el stinko.
parole.testo: From many Spanish or Italian words that end in o. This ending in such Spanish or Italian words generally derives from -um, the accusative singular inflectional ending for masculine and neuter nouns in Latin.

parole.significato: To lower (the sail of a ship, particularly the topsail).

parole.significato: A drinking establishment, often specifically of the type found in Latin America.
parole.testo: From Spanish cantina, from Italian cantina. Doublet of canteen.

parole.significato: Meat or fish that has been scored and broiled.
parole.testo: The noun is derived from Spanish carbonada (“carbonized”) (from carbonar (“to carbonize”)) + -ado (suffix forming past participles of regular verbs ending in -ar). Carbonada appears to have been modelled after Italian carbonata (“coal pile; stew of beef in red wine”), from carbone (“coal; charcoal”)

parole.significato: A large sheet of colored paper (usually in rolls).
parole.testo: From Spanish cartulina, from Italian cartolina, ultimately from carta (“paper”) + -lina. Compare Tagalog kartulina and Portuguese cartolina.

parole.significato: Any goods which are illicit or illegal to possess.
parole.testo: From Spanish contrabanda (modern spelling contrabando), from Italian contrabando (modern spelling contrabbando), from contra (“against”) + bando (“ban”), and reinforced by French contrebande.

parole.significato: A dish made by boiling bread in water and combining the pulp with milk, stock, butter or sometimes egg yolks.

parole.testo: From Spanish panatela, the name of a long thin biscuit, from the Italian diminutive panatella, which ultimately derives from Latin pānis (“bread”).

parole.testo: Unadapted borrowing from Mexican Spanish piñata, from piña (“pinecone”), from Latin pinea, because its paper cover (on traditional making) resembles one. Alternatively from Spanish via Italian pignatta (“clay pot”), from a Chinese custom allegedly introduced by Marco Polo.

parole.significato: Relating to or characteristic of early spring.
parole.testo: Probably from Spanish primavera (“springtime”) or Italian primavera (“springtime”), ultimately from Latin prima vera, + -al.

parole.significato: A Mexican sauce made chiefly of tomatillos.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Spanish salsa verde and Italian salsa verde, both meaning literally “green sauce”.

parole.significato: A trick-taking card game, originally from Italy.
parole.testo: From Spanish tute, previously from Italian tutti.

parole.significato: Long live ... ! (used to express acclaim or support).
parole.testo: Borrowed from Spanish viva and Italian viva.
